title: Reverse String
description: Brute force to optimized: a separate reversed array versus two pointers swapping in place.

blocks.text: Given an array of characters s, reverse it in place, using only O(1) extra space.

blocks.caption: Two pointers swap characters from both ends, converging toward the middle

blocks.text: Given an array of characters s, reverse it in place, using only O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: Analogy: Flipping a Row of Cards End for End
blocks.text: Like flipping a row of face up cards so the whole sequence reads backward, done directly by swapping matching pairs from opposite ends of the row toward the middle, with no second row needed.

blocks.caption: Reverse the array of characters directly in place, no extra array needed

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Reversing the order of every character","\"o\", \"l\", \"l\", \"e\", \"h\"","Each character's new position is exactly mirrored from its original position around the array's center"],["Answer","[\"o\", \"l\", \"l\", \"e\", \"h\"]","Every character has swapped places with its mirror-image partner"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s with a single character
A single character array is trivially its own reverse, unchanged.

Before building any new array, notice that reversing is really just a set of position swaps: the character at position i and the character at the mirrored position from the end simply need to trade places, for every i up to the halfway point.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Reversing an array is equivalent to swapping the first element with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on, meeting in the middle, since that is literally what "reversed order" means.

Observation 2: Since every swap only ever touches two positions that are already inside the original array, no second array is ever needed to hold intermediate results, the swap can happen directly in place.

Observation 3: A pointer starting at index 0 and another starting at the last index, both moving one step toward each other after every swap, visits exactly the n divided by 2 pairs that need swapping, and no more, stopping the moment they meet or cross.

Observation 4: Continuing past the point where the two pointers meet would simply undo the swaps just made, or swap the middle element with itself uselessly, so the loop must stop strictly before that happens.

Whenever a transformation is really a set of mirrored position swaps around a center, use two pointers starting at both ends and converging inward, swapping once per step, rather than building any new structure.

This is the most fundamental instance of the two-pointer-converging-from-both-ends pattern, and recognizing it here makes the same structure easy to spot in related problems like palindrome checks and array rotations.
Build a brand new array by reading the characters from the end backward, then copy that new array back over the original.

items: Build a new array by reading s from the last character to the first.
Copy the new array back over the original s.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The reversed sequence is constructed entirely separately, reading the original from back to front, before touching the original array at all.
The copy-back loop only runs after the entire reversed array has been built, since copying while still reading from the original in reverse could otherwise read from a position already overwritten.
Both loops run the full length of s, since every single position, not just half, needs to be visited when building and then copying an entirely separate array.

blocks.text: Reading the characters backward into a new array and copying it back correctly reverses the array.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), for building and copying the reversed array.
Space: O(n), for the separate reversed array, which the problem explicitly wants to avoid.
Limitation: reversing does not actually require a second array at all. Swapping characters directly from opposite ends, moving inward, produces the exact same result without any extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force builds an entire second array just to hold values that are already sitting somewhere in the original, at the exact mirrored position. Since a swap only ever needs the two positions directly involved, there is no need to ever hold the full reversed sequence anywhere at once, each pair can be exchanged directly and independently of every other pair. Recognizing that reversal decomposes into exactly n divided by 2 independent pairwise swaps, not one continuous rebuild, replaces the extra array with two simple index pointers that walk toward each other, swapping as they go and needing nothing beyond a single temporary variable per swap.

Use two pointers, one starting at the front and one at the back. Repeatedly swap the characters at the two pointers, then move the front pointer forward and the back pointer backward, stopping once they meet or cross in the middle.
Two pointers converging from both ends, swapping as they go.

blocks.caption: Optimized: two pointers swap characters from both ends, converging toward the middle

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each pointer moves inward at most n over 2 times.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional array is used.

Swapping the position i with its mirrored position from the end, for every i up to but not including the midpoint, covers every pair that reversal requires exactly once, with no pair repeated and none skipped, since the left pointer and right pointer are always exact mirror images of each other around the array's center by construction. Stopping once left is no longer strictly less than right guarantees the loop halts exactly when every pair has been swapped, whether the array has even length, pointers cross without landing on the same index, or odd length, pointers meet exactly at the single unmoved middle element.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Array length parity","What happens at the middle"],"rows":[["Even","The two pointers cross without ever pointing at the same index; every character is swapped with its partner"],["Odd","The two pointers meet at the single middle index, which correctly never needs to be swapped with itself"]]}

items: left and right start at index 0 and length minus 1, the two true ends of the array, before any swaps have occurred.

The loop condition, left strictly less than right, is what prevents the middle element of an odd-length array from being uselessly swapped with itself, and prevents an even-length array's two pointers from swapping the same pair twice.
The swap itself exchanges the two end characters using a temporary variable, or a language's built-in tuple-swap syntax, affecting only those two positions and nothing else.
left is incremented and right is decremented together, once per iteration, guaranteeing the two pointers always advance symmetrically toward the center.

blocks.text: This is the most fundamental application of the "two pointers converging from both ends" pattern, the same technique used to check palindromes, reverse ranges within a larger structure, and rotate arrays.

items: Using a loop condition that allows the pointers to be equal instead of strictly less than, which for an even length array would swap the middle two characters back to their original positions on a redundant extra iteration, or for an odd length array would attempt to swap the middle character with itself unnecessarily.
Building an unnecessary temporary array when swapping in place is both simpler and meets the O(1) space requirement directly.
Forgetting to advance both pointers together after a swap, which would either skip a needed swap or repeat one, breaking the mirrored correspondence between left and right.

items: Mention this exact two pointer swap pattern as the foundation for a whole family of related problems, so the interviewer sees the broader pattern recognition, not just a solution to this one problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Reverse a sequence in place, O(1) space" points toward two pointers starting at both ends, swapping and converging toward the middle, stopping once they meet or cross.

items: How would you reverse only a subrange of the array, not the whole thing? The exact same two-pointer technique applies, just initializing left and right to the subrange's start and end indices instead of the full array's.

How does this relate to checking whether a string is a palindrome? A palindrome check uses the identical two-pointer converging structure, just comparing characters for equality instead of swapping them.

What if the array were a singly linked list instead of an array? Two pointers from both ends no longer work directly, since a singly linked list cannot be traversed backward in O(1); reversing a linked list instead requires re-pointing each node's next reference while walking forward only once.
The foundational example of the "two pointers converging from both ends" pattern, directly reused, with a comparison instead of a swap, in Valid Palindrome.
Same in-place swap technique used inside Rotate Array's three-reversal trick, applied there to sub-ranges instead of the whole array.
Same "stop once pointers meet or cross" loop-termination discipline needed in every converging two-pointer problem, regardless of what happens at each step.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Two pointers converging from both ends, swapping in place
Core Idea: Reversal decomposes into exactly n divided by 2 independent mirrored-position swaps, each handled directly without any auxiliary array
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: Any transformation that pairs up mirrored positions around a center can be done with two converging pointers instead of building a new structure
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Swap the ends, walk inward, stop when they meet
